title: How To Respond To A Sudden Increase In Misbehavior sbehavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses moments when unexpected events — a fire drill, a Wi-Fi outage, hard rain — trigger a sudden spike in student misbehavior, and lays out a three-step protocol for correcting it without showing frustration. Step one, review: recap objectively and without naming names exactly what happened, like a neutral reporter. Step two, state: simply and calmly declare that the behavior isn't acceptable and won't be, then pause and let the words sit. Step three, practice: have the class demonstrate the correct behavior for 30 seconds to a minute, modeling it first if needed, so they prove understanding rather than just hearing about it. He recommends delaying this three-step process by at least a couple of hours, ideally to the next day, so students can reflect with a 'calm heart and fresh set of eyes' rather than in the emotional aftermath of the incident, and stresses ending the process with praise and moving on as if nothing happened, since the responsibility now shifts entirely to students for next time.
points: Follow a three-step protocol after a sudden misbehavior spike: review what happened objectively, state plainly that it isn't acceptable, then have students practice the correct behavior.
Deliberately delay the review-state-practice sequence by at least a couple of hours, ideally to the next day, so students can reflect with a calm mind.
During the 'review' step, recap facts like a neutral reporter without naming names and without showing displeasure.
Give students 30 seconds to a minute to physically demonstrate the correct behavior, modeling it first if their age requires it.
End the process with praise and move on as if nothing happened — the burden now shifts entirely to students to handle it better next time.
quotes: Anything unexpected can stir up excitability and incite an increase misbehavior. And you can’t run away scared. No matter what, you still must follow through calmly.
Review what happened like a small town newspaper reporter. Don’t mention any names. Just stick to the facts and recap in detail, leaving nothing out.

Step two is to simply state that such behavior isn’t okay and will never be accepted. Even though you’ve already taught your classroom management plan, and have followed through consistently, they need to hear you say it.
Give your ‘go’ signal and allow 30 seconds to a minute of correct, mature behavior. Yes, it may just be sitting in their seats quietly.
It’s important to mention, however, that it’s best not to complete the three steps right away. Allow for at least a couple of hours. The next day is often best.
After step three, praise them for doing it right and then move on to the next lesson or activity as if nothing happened.
